div.p: Three-dimensional network on chips (3D NoCs) have been developed to achieve high computation and communication throughput for the growing demands of applications. But with increased applications and cores, real-time task management for 3D NoCs becomes a major challenge. The difficulty of this process is due to the precedence constraint between applications and the communication overhead between cores. In this paper, we propose an on-line real-time task management framework for 3D NoCs to minimize the makespan of each application and minimize the communication overhead of systems, in order to meet the quality of service requirements and maximize system performance. Schedulability and scalability of the proposed methodology is evaluated by a series of experiments, with encouraging results.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: To meet the growing processing demands of many applications, three-dimensional network-on-chips (3D NoCs) [1], [2], [3] are used for greater computation and communication throughput. These systems are used for a wide variety of applications simultaneously executed with quality of service requirements. In contrast to the traditional high performance single core, the number of cores is dramatically increased in the 3D NoCs for power efficiency. The need for real-time task management is increasing for 3D NoCs in order to maximize system utilization and to meet timing constraints.

Most of the research on task management in 2D-NoCs has been done in the past decade. Some of these works present hardware-software co-synthesis algorithms to allocate processing elements and manage tasks to minimize energy or maximize system performance, e.g., [4], [5], and another work [6] proposes a dynamic task allocation methodology to minimize the communication cost of applications by analyzing communication properties without computation resources consideration. For 3D NoCs, most prior work has proposed processor allocation for mesh-connected cores to minimize the communication cost, without considering quality of service e.g. [7], [8], [9].

This study is motivated by the demand for real-time task management for 3D NoCs, and it presents an on-line realtime task management framework to quickly dispatch and schedule tasks with precedence constraint for the given 3D NoCs. The system performance is improved by eliminating the communication overhead with critical path consideration and reducing the communication contention with floor planning consideration. The schedulability and scalability of the proposed methodology are evaluated by a series of experiments, which present encouraging results.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II introduces the system model and the problem definition. Section III proposes the framework and algorithms of real-time task management for 3D NoCs. Section IV presents the performance evaluation details, and Section V offers conclusions. This study investigates real-time task management for the three-dimensional network on chips (3D NoCs). In Fig 1, the 3D NoCs [2], [3] is composed of N X ×N Y ×N Z homogenous cores which are interconnected by a 3D mesh network, where N X , N Y , and N Z are the number of cores in X-axis, Y-axis and Z-axis, respectively. Each core allocated in i-th row, j-th column, and k-th layer is denoted as P k i,j . The link channel connection between P k i,j and P k i+1,j is denoted as Lx k i,j , and the link channel connection between P k i,j and P k i,j+1 is denoted as Ly k i,j . The proposed system consists of a set of tasks Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ m }. Each task τ i is modeled by a task graph T G i as shown in Fig 2 . Each vertex represents a subtask τ i,j , and each directed edge e i j,k represents a data transaction and a precedence constraint between τ i,j and τ i,k . The execution time and deadline of the subtask τ i,j are denoted as c i,j and d i,j , respectively. The transmission time for each data transaction e j,k is denoted as t j,k . In contrast to task execution, the data transaction between tasks could be eliminated by clustering tasks in the same core. Thus the response time of each task could be improved by reducing the communication overhead. In this paper, the online real-time task management framework is presented as shown in Fig 3 . Given the new task and the 3D NoCs, a heuristic to cluster tasks in order to minimize the communication overhead is presented. The number of cores is increased dramatically in the 3D NoCs for better performance, but this causes more communication contention in the system. We then present a heuristic to assign tasks into cores in order to minimize the communication contention, and this improves system utilization. In this study, we assume that each task and data transaction is scheduled according to Earliest Deadline First (EDF) [11] in cores and channels/TSVs, respectively. According to the given deadline of sink subtask, the deadline of each subtask and data transaction are assigned according to As Late As Possible (ALAP) for the schedulability test. If the new task passes the schedulability test, the task is allocated into the system; otherwise, the task is rejected.

div.head: A. Task Cluster
div.p: The algorithm of task cluster is shown in Algorithm 1. To minimize the makespan of each task, we cluster subtasks in the critical path to eliminate the communication overhead between cores. To reduce the communication overhead efficiently, we choose the subtasks with the maximum data transactions (maximum degrees), and then cluster the corresponding predecessor subtasks and following subtasks in the same cluster (Steps 2 -23). After some subtasks are clustered, the critical path of the task might be different (Step 17). If the critical path is changed and the subtasks of this critical path not been assigned to a cluster, the corresponding subtasks are assigned to another cluster. By doing so, the execution contention between subtasks can be eliminated for shorter marksman of the task (Steps 24 -26). The procedure is terminated when each subtask in the system has been assigned to a corresponding cluster. The time complexity of Algorithm 1 is O(nm 3 ), where n is the number of task set and m is the number of subtasks.

div.head: B. Task Assignment
div.p: After task clustering, we then propose the task assignment algorithm to minimize communication contention, as shown in Algorithm 2.

To reduce the makespan of each task, we assign clusters belonging to the critical path into vertically stacked cores. By doing so, the data transactions between cores are transferred through the TSV channel, which has better performance than link channels [12] (Steps 2 -12). Each cluster is assigned to one of the cores with more link channels in order to reduce the communication overhead between clusters. Therefore, we first assign clusters into the central core in the 3D NoCs, i.e. P 0 NX /2,NY /2 . First, we find an assigned cluster with out-degree larger than or equal to 1, and then assign all the following clusters of it to the closest horizontally leveled cores (Steps 25 -42). By doing so, the communication overhead between clusters is minimized. If the following cluster with in-degree larger than 1 and all predecessors of the corresponding cluster are assigned, the corresponding cluster is assigned to the core with minimum communication cost among all cores assigned by all predecessor clusters (Steps 43 -54), thereby reducing the communication cost from all predecessor clusters. If the following cluster communicates only with the assigned cluster (i.e. with in-degree as 1), the cluster is assigned into the closest horizontally leveled core with minimum utilization (Steps 55 -63) in order to maximize the schedulability. div.head: A. Experimental Environment
div.p: In this section, we evaluate our 3D NoCs real-time task management 3DRT by extensive simulations and compare it with the greedy method. The greedy algorithm assigns all subtasks in the current critical path to the same core, and the core with minimum distance to the prior picked one is chosen first. The first chosen core is the central core of 3D NoCs, where is P 0 NX /2,NY /2 . The two performance metrics considered in this paper are: the response time divided by the execution time and the feasible ratio. The Response time Divided by Execution time (RDE), is defined as the ratio of the response time of each job under the evaluated algorithm to the execution time of the critical path of the job. The results are separately averaged for each task in the given set. If the ratio is less, the performance is better because the execution contention and communication contention are less. The feasible ratio is the ratio of the number of task sets without deadline violation under the evaluated algorithm to the number of total task sets generated.

The synthetic task graphs are generated by the graph generator "Task Graph for Free"(TGFF) [13]. Algorithms are evaluated for a set of task graphs with the number of subtasks ranging from 25 to 300, and each graph has 1 to 3 in-degrees and 5 to 8 out-degrees. Each task graph is represented by (n, m), where n and m are the number of in-degrees and outdegrees, respectively. The execution time of each subtask and data transaction ranges from 5 to 8 time units, and the deadline of each task is set as 2 times the total execution times of all subtasks and data transactions. The 3D NoCs with 6×6×2 and 3 × 3 × 2 homogenous cores is considered in the experiment, and the router latency is 1 time unit. For each setting, 100 task sets are generated to average the experimental results. Figure 6 shows the feasible ratios of 3DRT and greedy algorithms, considering the task set with 50 subtasks and a 3D NoCs with 6 × 6 × 2 homogenous cores. The vertical axis represents the feasible ratio, and the horizontal axis represents the number of in/out degrees of the given task set. As shown in Fig 6, the results show that 3DRT achieves better schedulability than the greedy algorithm. In addition, the feasible ratio decreases, as the number of in-degrees or outdegrees is increasing. This is because more communication contention and reduced system performance occurs when the number of data transactions is increasing. The performance gap between 3DRT and the greedy algorithm are increased as the number of data transactions are increased, indicating that 3DRT has better scalability than the greedy algorithm.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: Figures 7(a) and (b) show the feasible ratios of 3DRT and greedy algorithms, when the number of homogenous cores in 3D NoCs are 6 × 6 × 2 and 3 × 3 × 2, respectively. The vertical axis represents the feasible ratio, and the horizontal axis represents the total utilization of the task set. Although the schedualbility of 3DRT is decreased as the number of degrees Figure 8 shows the RDE of 3DRT and greedy algorithms, when the number of subtasks are 50, 100, 200, and 300, respectively. The total utilization in this experiment ranges from 1.3 to 6.8. The vertical axis represents RDE, and the horizontal axis represents the number of in/out degrees of the given task set. In this experiment, only feasible tasks are considered. The higher ratio represents more contentions. As shown in Fig 8(a), the RDE of 3DRT ranges from 1.12 to 1.33, and the RDE of greedy ranges from 1.46 to 1.78. The results show that 3DRT manages communication contention efficiently. Compared Figs. 8(a) and (b), although the performance of 3DRT is increased with the number of subtasks, the performance gap between 3DRT and the greedy algorithm is increased. This shows that 3DRT also more effectively manages the task contention in each core than the greedy algorithm. For example, when the task graph with 8 out-degrees and 1 in-degree, the RDE of 3DRT are 1.29 and 1.47 in Figs. 8(a) and (b), respectively. The RDE of the greedy algorithm are 1.77 and 2.16 in Figs. 8(a) and (b), respectively. When there are more than 200 subtasks, there is no feasible task for the greedy algorithm. Therefore, only the results of 3DRT are shown in Figs. 8(c) and (d) to show the scalability of 3DRT. As shown in Fig. 8(d), the RDE increases dramatically when the in-degree of the task is 1. This is because it is hard to eliminate the communication contention by task assignment if all data transactions are requested from the same subtask.

V. CONCLUSIONS This paper proposes an on-line real-time task management framework for three-dimensional network on chips. To meet the real-time constraints of each task, the communication overhead is eliminated by the task clustering with critical path consideration. Moreover, communication contention is reduced by task assignment with floor planning consideration. Schedulability of each task is guaranteed by the existing realtime task scheduler in each core and link, which is supposed as the earliest deadline first in this paper. The experimental results show that the proposed framework achieves better system performance by efficiently managing communication and task contentions.
